Twelve years ago, the week before I left Australia, I couldn't sleep. So I [made a little D3 map](../2014-08-01-a-chapter-closes-a-chapter-opens/) of every flight I'd taken during my astrophysics postdoc — Dallas to Los Angeles to Melbourne, and everywhere that came after.

That map is gone now. It lived on bl.ocks.org, a little service for sharing D3 sketches, and when bl.ocks shut down it took the visualization with it. The old post still exists, but where the map used to be there's a dead embed.

::: {.column-margin}
bl.ocks.org rendered visualizations straight from GitHub gists. The service went away but my gist survived.
:::

I finally got around to fixing it. And since I was starting from scratch anyway, I pulled in my logbook of every flight I have a record of back to 2005.

::: {.column-page}
![Every flight I have a record of, 2005–2026. The map is Pacific-centered; arc opacity stacks, so the routes I've flown most often glow brightest.](/assets/images/flights/flights-map.svg)
:::

There's most of my adult life in that tangle. The bright knot on the right is home base drifting around the United States — Dallas, where I grew up; San Diego for grad school; and the dense little triangle of the Bay Area commute I could now draw from memory. The long arcs sweeping down across the Pacific are the Australia years. The threads reaching to Chile and Hawaii are observing runs — nights at the VLT in the Atacama and Keck on Mauna Kea, which at the time felt like the most exotic commute imaginable.

::: {.column-margin}
The faint lines to Santiago and Antofagasta are the road to Paranal; the ones to Honolulu and Kona are Keck.
:::

Seeing it all at once does something the individual trips never did. Each flight was just a flight — a red-eye, a layover, a bad sandwich. Drawn together they make a shape, and the shape is recognizably a life: where I came from, what I was chasing, who I was flying to see.

## How it's made (this time)

A note for anyone tempted to build one of these.

The 2014 version died for a reason worth remembering: it leaned on someone else's server. This time I made a single static SVG (with help from Claude). 
It's generated from my flight log by a [small Python program](https://github.com/jbwhit/website/tree/main/scripts/flights). As long as the page renders, the map renders.

The other thing I was careful about: a flight log is more sensitive than it looks. The only data that ships is the part that draws the picture: the airports, and how many times I've flown each route. No dates, no booking details, nothing that says where I'll be next Tuesday.
